cloze.text: A traumatic ulcer is a localized loss of oral epithelium caused by direct {{c1::mechanical}}, {{c2::thermal}}, or {{c3::chemical}} injury to the oral mucosa.
cloze.extra: e.g., biting, sharp food, ill-fitting dentures, dental instruments

cloze.text: Traumatic ulcers occur on BOTH {{c1::movable}} mucosa (cheeks, lips, soft palate) and {{c2::unmovable}} mucosa (hard palate, gingiva, dorsal tongue).
cloze.extra: Contrast: aphthous ulcers occur ONLY on movable, nonkeratinized mucosa.

cloze.text: Appearance of a traumatic ulcer: well-defined ulcer with a {{c1::yellowish base}} and {{c2::red halo}}.
A traumatic ulcer is painful and heals within {{c1::7–14 days}} after {{c2::removing the irritant}}.
An aspirin burn is a {{c1::chemical burn}} of the oral mucosa caused by direct placement of aspirin, due to the acidic nature of {{c2::acetylsalicylic acid}}.
cloze.extra: It is a type of traumatic ulcer.

cloze.text: Aspirin burns are most common on the {{c1::buccal mucosa, vestibule, or gingiva}} near the {{c2::painful tooth}}.
Appearance of an aspirin burn: {{c1::white, necrotic}} lesion that may slough off, leaving a {{c2::red, painful}} base.
An aphthous ulcer (canker sore) is triggered by {{c1::stress, hormones, nutritional deficiencies}}, or unknown triggers.
cloze.extra: e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency, school stress. "Aphthous" means eruption or ulcer.

cloze.text: Aphthous ulcers occur ONLY on {{c1::movable, nonkeratinized}} mucosa (labial/buccal mucosa, vestibule, ventral/lateral tongue, soft palate, nasopharynx).
cloze.extra: Board favourite: NOT on attached gingiva or hard palate (keratinized) — that points to herpes or trauma instead.

cloze.text: Appearance of an aphthous ulcer: small, round or oval ulcer with a {{c1::yellowish-white center}} and {{c2::red halo}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: think of the Target logo — white center, then a red halo. (Shopping at Target = stress reliever.)

cloze.text: A (minor) aphthous ulcer is painful, heals spontaneously in 7–14 days with {{c1::no scarring}}; treated with {{c2::topical steroids}} or rinses to reduce discomfort.
Of the three aphthous ulcer types, {{c1::minor}} aphthous ulcers are the most common and {{c2::herpetiform}} aphthous ulcers the least common.
Location by aphthous type: minor and major aphthae occur on {{c1::movable mucosa}}; herpetiform aphthae can occur {{c2::anywhere in the oral cavity}}.
Healing: minor and herpetiform aphthae heal in 7–10 days with no scarring; {{c1::major}} aphthae take {{c2::several weeks}}, often with scarring.
Pain: minor aphthae = {{c1::mild to moderate}}; major = more severe; herpetiform = {{c2::very painful}} due to numerous small ulcers.
Associated factors: minor aphthae — {{c1::stress, minor trauma}}; major aphthae — {{c2::immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV)}}, systemic disease; herpetiform — unknown.
Despite the name, herpetiform aphthous ulcers are NOT caused by the {{c1::herpes virus}}.
Treatment: minor aphthae — topical corticosteroids, supportive care; major — {{c1::topical or systemic corticosteroids}}; herpetiform — {{c2::topical tetracycline}} or corticosteroids.
Frictional keratosis is a {{c1::benign}}, reactive lesion where the mucosa develops a thickened layer of {{c2::keratin}} in response to chronic mechanical irritation.
cloze.extra: e.g., cheek biting, sharp teeth, dental appliances. Keratin = tough fibrous protein in the outer layer of skin, hair, nails and oral mucosa lining.

cloze.text: {{c1::Linea alba}} is considered a form of frictional keratosis.
Frictional keratosis appears as a {{c1::white patch}} with {{c2::no ulceration}} at the site of irritation, in areas subject to repeated trauma.
Frictional keratosis is asymptomatic and {{c1::resolves once the trauma is eliminated}}.
WakeUpMemory: multiple myeloma = {{c1::punched-out}} radiographic lesions ("multiple holes").
A pyogenic granuloma is a reactive red or purple, soft, elevated mass that bleeds easily due to its {{c1::high vascularity}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is often called a {{c1::pregnancy tumor}} (though not always related to pregnancy).
Cause of pyogenic granuloma: {{c1::hormonal influence}} (typically regresses after childbirth); in non-pregnant people, {{c2::local irritation (plaque or trauma)}}.
Pyogenic granuloma is most often on the {{c1::gingiva}}, but may also occur on lips, tongue, buccal mucosa, or skin (hands, fingers, face).
Pyogenic granuloma appearance: smooth, {{c1::lobulated}}, dark {{c2::reddish}}; {{c3::painless}} but bleeds easily.
cloze.extra: Treatment: heals on its own; surgery may be needed.

cloze.text: Urticaria and angioedema are {{c1::allergic reactions}} triggered by {{c2::histamine}}, causing swelling from fluid leaking into tissues.

{{c1::Urticaria (hives)}} = multiple raised, red or pale, well-defined, itchy skin patches that appear suddenly; {{c2::angioedema}} = deeper tissue swelling, especially around the lips, eyes, or throat.
Urticaria is intensely itchy ({{c1::pruritus}}); angioedema is usually {{c2::not itchy}} but may cause tightness or discomfort.
Angioedema involving the airway may cause {{c1::breathing difficulty}}; severe cases may require {{c2::epinephrine}} and emergency intervention.
Urticaria/angioedema treatment: {{c1::antihistamines}}, with {{c2::corticosteroids}} for more persistent cases.

Contact dermatitis is inflammation of the skin or oral mucosa caused by {{c1::direct contact with allergens}} or irritants, e.g., latex gloves, metal in dental appliances, toothpaste flavoring agents.
Contact dermatitis is limited to the {{c1::area of contact}}; appearance: swelling, redness, itching, burning, sometimes a smooth shiny surface.
Contact dermatitis is a {{c1::Type IV (delayed)}} hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized {{c2::T-cells}}, with symptoms appearing {{c3::hours to days}} after exposure.
A hematoma is a localized accumulation of {{c1::blood}} within tissue from ruptured blood vessels, typically after trauma or injury (e.g., a dental needle).
In dentistry, hematoma is common after a {{c1::PSA (posterior superior alveolar)}} nerve block, where the {{c2::pterygoid venous plexus}} may be punctured.
cloze.extra: Location: buccal mucosa, vestibule, or near the injection site.

cloze.text: A hematoma appears as a {{c1::dark swelling}}; it resolves on its own within {{c2::a few days to weeks}}, and {{c3::cold compresses}} reduce initial swelling.
A mucocele is a {{c1::pseudocyst}} (not lined by epithelium) that forms when mucin from a ruptured {{c2::minor}} salivary gland duct leaks into connective tissue, typically after trauma (lip biting).
Mucoceles are most often found on the {{c1::lower lip}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "seal the lips" — keep your mucoCELE a secret. Also buccal mucosa, ventral tongue, soft palate, retromolar pad, upper lip.

cloze.text: Mucoceles can occur anywhere minor salivary glands exist — i.e., everywhere except the {{c1::anterior hard palate}} and {{c2::attached gingiva}}.
Mucocele appearance: soft, {{c1::bluish}}, dome-shaped, less than {{c2::1.5 cm}} in diameter.
cloze.extra: Asymptomatic; may resolve on its own; surgical excision if needed.

cloze.text: A ranula is a larger, bluish, fluctuant lesion on the {{c1::floor of the mouth}}, caused by trauma or blockage of a {{c2::major}} salivary gland — most often the {{c3::sublingual}} gland.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: ranula = "frog" in Latin — the swelling resembles a frog's translucent underbelly.

cloze.text: The sublingual gland drains via {{c1::Bartholin's and Rivinus}} ducts and produces ~{{c2::5–10%}} of saliva, mostly {{c3::mucous}}.
A ranula is larger and deeper than a mucocele and may {{c1::displace the tongue}}; it may need {{c2::surgery}}.
Sialolithiasis is a {{c1::calcified mass (stone)}} in the ducts of major or minor salivary glands.
Sialoliths occur most often in the {{c1::submandibular}} gland, which drains through {{c2::Wharton's}} duct.
A sialolith causes pain and swelling especially during {{c1::meals}}, when salivary flow increases and saliva creates pressure around the stone.
cloze.extra: Appearance: firm, localized swelling.

cloze.text: Small sialoliths may pass with {{c1::hydration or stimulation}} (e.g., lemon slices); larger stones may require {{c2::surgical removal}}.
Sjögren's syndrome is a chronic {{c1::autoimmune}} disease in which the immune system attacks the {{c2::salivary}} and {{c3::lacrimal}} glands.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Sjögren's = Sahara syndrome — dries up saliva and tears.

cloze.text: Sjögren's affects the salivary glands, especially the {{c1::parotid}}, and may cause {{c2::bilateral}} parotid swelling in about half of cases.
Sjögren's causes {{c1::xerostomia}} (dry mouth) and {{c2::xerophthalmia}} (dry eyes).
Xerostomia + xerophthalmia together = {{c1::sicca}} syndrome, which may also occur in conditions other than Sjögren's.
Sjögren's patients may have difficulty speaking and swallowing and a burning sensation; management: artificial saliva, {{c1::fluoride products}}, and {{c2::antifungals}} if candidiasis occurs.
Sjögren's is confirmed by a {{c1::minor salivary gland biopsy}} (typically from the lip) and blood tests (positive {{c2::rheumatoid factor}} or autoantibodies).
Median rhomboid glossitis is a red, flat or slightly raised lesion in the {{c1::midline of the dorsal tongue}}, just in front of the {{c2::circumvallate papillae}}.
Median rhomboid glossitis appears well-defined, {{c1::rhomboid (diamond-shaped)}}, and {{c2::smooth}}, red due to loss of {{c3::filiform}} papillae.
Median rhomboid glossitis is linked to chronic {{c1::Candida albicans}}; more common in {{c2::immunocompromised}} individuals or denture wearers.
cloze.extra: Asymptomatic/mild burning; no treatment needed — antifungals if Candida is involved.

cloze.text: Geographic tongue is a benign inflammatory condition with multiple {{c1::red patches}} surrounded by {{c2::white or yellowish borders}}, giving a map-like appearance.
Geographic tongue affects the {{c1::dorsal and lateral}} surfaces of the tongue.
In geographic tongue, the red depapillated zones are where {{c1::filiform}} papillae are lost, bordered by regenerating or {{c2::hyperkeratotic}} tissue.
Geographic tongue is asymptomatic but may burn with {{c1::spicy or acidic foods}}; no treatment unless symptoms persist. May be linked to stress, hormonal changes, or {{c2::psoriasis}}.
Hairy tongue is a benign condition caused by {{c1::elongation of the filiform papillae}} on the dorsal tongue due to {{c2::keratin}} buildup.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: normally saliva and chewing give the papillae a daily "haircut"; antibiotics, dry mouth or smoking stop that, so the "hairs" grow long.

cloze.text: Hairy tongue projections may be brown, black, yellow, or green, depending on trapped {{c1::bacteria, food, tobacco, or pigments}}.
Hairy tongue is linked to poor oral hygiene, smoking, alcohol, and medications such as {{c1::antibiotics}}, {{c2::corticosteroids}}, and anticholinergics.
Hairy tongue is usually asymptomatic but may cause halitosis, gagging, or bad taste; managed by {{c1::tongue brushing}}, improved hygiene, and eliminating contributing factors.
Hairy leukoplakia is a white lesion typically on the {{c1::lateral borders}} of the tongue.
Hairy leukoplakia is caused by {{c1::Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)}}, which is human herpesvirus {{c2::4}}; the virus infects epithelial cells, causing {{c3::hyperkeratosis}}.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: >90% of adults carry EBV (the "kissing disease" virus, spread through saliva); it stays for life and can trigger hairy leukoplakia when immunity is weak.

cloze.text: Hairy leukoplakia appears as a white, corrugated, "hairy" plaque that {{c1::cannot be wiped off}}.
Hairy leukoplakia is common in {{c1::HIV-positive}} or immunosuppressed patients; it is asymptomatic and {{c2::not premalignant}}.
cloze.extra: May need medical intervention.

cloze.text: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is a {{c1::congenital}} condition in which the {{c2::lingual frenum}} is unusually short, thick, or tight, limiting tongue movement.
Ankyloglossia may cause difficulty with speech, breastfeeding, and oral hygiene, or contribute to {{c1::gingival recession}}; treated by {{c2::frenectomy}} (surgical removal or release of a frenum).
Fissured tongue is a benign anatomical variation with deep {{c1::grooves or cracks}} on the {{c2::dorsal}} surface of the tongue.
Fissured tongue is asymptomatic, with mild burning if food debris is trapped; no treatment needed — {{c1::gentle tongue cleaning}} advised.
Fissured tongue is associated with aging, dry mouth, genetic predisposition, and {{c1::Down syndrome}}.
Nicotine stomatitis is a benign, reactive lesion of the {{c1::hard palate}} caused by chronic exposure to {{c2::heat}} — pipes, cigars, or very hot beverages — not from nicotine itself.
Nicotine stomatitis starts as a diffuse {{c1::redness}}, then becomes a diffuse {{c2::white}}, opalescent thickening with small {{c3::red dots}} (inflamed minor salivary gland openings).
Nicotine stomatitis is asymptomatic and {{c1::reversible}} if the heat source is eliminated early.
cloze.extra: The book adds: can become cancerous.

cloze.text: Tobacco pouch keratosis forms where {{c1::smokeless tobacco}} (chewing tobacco or snuff) is habitually placed — most commonly the {{c2::mucobuccal fold of the mandibular vestibule}}.
Tobacco pouch keratosis appears {{c1::white}}, folded, or leathery; asymptomatic, may regress after stopping tobacco; may require {{c2::biopsy}}.
Smoker's melanosis is a benign {{c1::pigmentation}} of the oral mucosa caused by stimulation of {{c2::melanocytes}} from chronic tobacco smoke (like skin tanning in sun).
Smoker's melanosis appears as diffuse or patchy {{c1::brown}} discoloration in smoke-exposed areas; asymptomatic, not premalignant, can improve with {{c2::smoking cessation}}.
Epulis fissuratum is a folded {{c1::overgrowth of fibrous tissue}} in the vestibule caused by an {{c2::ill-fitting denture}}.
Epulis fissuratum appears as {{c1::redundant folds}} of tissue in the vestibule, commonly on the {{c2::edge}} of a poorly fitting denture; can be ulcerated or inflamed.
Epulis fissuratum is asymptomatic (painful if ulcerated); treatment: {{c1::adjust the denture}}; may need surgical removal of tissue.
Papillary hyperplasia is a benign overgrowth of the {{c1::palatal}} mucosa from chronic denture irritation, especially when the denture is poorly cleaned or {{c2::never removed}} (lack of airflow).
cloze.extra: Often associated with Candida infection.

cloze.text: Papillary hyperplasia: small, red projections with a {{c1::cobblestone}} surface, typically on the {{c2::central hard palate}} beneath a maxillary denture.
Papillary hyperplasia is asymptomatic; teach {{c1::denture hygiene}} (cleaning, removal at night); may need {{c2::antifungal}} therapy.
Denture stomatitis is also called chronic {{c1::atrophic candidiasis}}.
Denture stomatitis is inflammation of the palatal mucosa and maxillary ridge beneath a removable denture caused by overgrowth of {{c1::Candida albicans}} due to poor denture hygiene.
Denture stomatitis appears as diffuse {{c1::redness}} confined to the area covered by the {{c2::denture base}}, most common on the hard palate and ridge under an {{c3::upper}} denture.
cloze.extra: Asymptomatic; teach denture hygiene (cleaning, removal at night); may need antifungal therapy.

cloze.text: A periapical granuloma is a chronic inflammatory lesion of {{c1::granulation tissue}} at the apex of a {{c2::non-vital}} tooth, caused by long-standing pulpal necrosis (deep decay or trauma).
A periapical granuloma shows a {{c1::radiolucency}} at the apex that is {{c2::indistinguishable}} on radiographs from a periapical cyst or abscess.
A periapical granuloma is asymptomatic (may cause mild pressure); treated with {{c1::root canal therapy}} or extraction.

A periapical (radicular) cyst is a true cyst at the apex of a {{c1::non-vital}} tooth; chronic inflammation stimulates the {{c2::epithelial rests of Malassez}} to form an epithelium-lined, fluid-filled cavity.
cloze.extra: Cause: pulpal necrosis from deep caries, trauma or large restorations.

cloze.text: A periapical cyst appears as a well-defined radiolucency at the apex of a non-vital tooth or at the site of an {{c1::extracted tooth}}.
A periapical cyst is {{c1::asymptomatic}}; treatment: endodontic therapy or extraction — it may resolve with proper root canal treatment.
The periapical (radicular) cyst is the {{c1::most common}} cyst in the oral cavity.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: periapical sounds like "popular".

cloze.text: A periapical abscess is a localized collection of {{c1::pus}} at the apex of a non-vital tooth, caused by {{c2::acute}} bacterial infection secondary to pulpal necrosis (deep caries, trauma, or periodontal disease).
Radiographically, a periapical abscess shows a {{c1::widened PDL space}} at early stages, progressing to a radiolucency at the root apex.
A periapical abscess causes {{c1::severe pain}} due to pressure, plus facial swelling; the tooth may feel {{c2::elevated}}, with a foul taste if it drains through a {{c3::sinus tract}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Abscess = pain — "ABSolutely hurts!"

cloze.text: Periapical abscess treatment: {{c1::drainage}}, antibiotics, and either root canal therapy or extraction.
Focal sclerosing osteomyelitis is also called {{c1::condensing osteitis}}.

Condensing osteitis is a chronic, low-grade inflammatory reaction at the apex of a {{c1::non-vital or inflamed}} tooth (deep caries or large restoration); the bone lays down extra {{c2::dense bone}} instead of inflaming.
Condensing osteitis occurs mostly in the {{c1::mandibular first molars}} of {{c2::young adults}}.
Condensing osteitis appears as a well-defined {{c1::radiopaque}} area extending from the root apex; no treatment is needed for the bone — treat or extract the tooth.
Alveolar osteitis (dry socket) is a post-extraction complication where the {{c1::blood clot}} is lost or fails to form, leaving {{c2::exposed bone}} in the socket.
Dry socket is most common after extraction of {{c1::mandibular third molars}}.
Dry socket appears as an empty socket with exposed bone, often {{c1::without pus or swelling}}.

A dentigerous (follicular) cyst is a developmental odontogenic cyst that forms around the {{c1::crown}} of an {{c2::unerupted or impacted}} tooth, with fluid between the {{c3::reduced enamel epithelium}} and the crown.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: dentigerous = impacted — car accident → dent → impact.

cloze.text: Dentigerous cysts occur mostly with impacted {{c1::mandibular third molars}} or {{c2::maxillary canines}}.
A dentigerous cyst is a well-defined {{c1::unilocular}} radiolucency attached at the {{c2::CEJ}}.
Dentigerous cysts are asymptomatic but large ones may {{c1::displace teeth}}; treated with {{c2::enucleation}} and removal of the involved tooth.
An eruption cyst forms over the crown of an {{c1::erupting}} tooth — most commonly over erupting {{c2::first permanent molars or incisors}}.
cloze.extra: Common in both primary and permanent dentitions.

cloze.text: An eruption cyst is a soft, dome-shaped, translucent to {{c1::bluish}} swelling; asymptomatic, no treatment — the tooth usually {{c2::erupts through the cyst}}.
cloze.extra: Fun fact: bluish because fluid or blood trapped under the mucosa makes a translucent or blood-tinged swelling.

cloze.text: A primordial cyst is a developmental cyst that arises where a tooth failed to develop — {{c1::instead of a tooth}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: primordial = failed teeth — like a primer coat with no final colour.

cloze.text: Primordial cysts are commonly in the {{c1::mandibular third molar}} region; a well-defined radiolucency, often discovered {{c2::incidentally}}; treated by surgical removal.
Pulpitis is inflammation of the dental pulp caused by a {{c1::carious infection}}; it can be {{c2::reversible or irreversible}}.
cloze.extra: Symptoms: pain. Involves extraction or root canal.

cloze.text: A {{c1::pulp polyp}} is an overgrowth of chronically inflamed pulp tissue that protrudes out of an open carious pulp chamber.
Pulp polyps occur most often in {{c1::molars}} with wide pulp chambers and appear as a {{c2::pink, fleshy}} mass of granulation tissue protruding from the pulp chamber.
Regional odontodysplasia ("{{c1::ghost teeth}}") is a rare developmental abnormality affecting {{c2::enamel, dentin, and pulp}} of one or more teeth.
cloze.extra: Caused by trauma, etc.

cloze.text: Regional odontodysplasia is usually {{c1::unilateral}}, in the same {{c2::quadrant}}, and can affect both primary and permanent teeth.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: a ghost haunts one corner — one section of the jaw.

cloze.text: In regional odontodysplasia, teeth are small, malformed, {{c1::hypoplastic}}, and may fail to erupt or erupt late.
Radiographically, regional odontodysplasia is "ghost-like": {{c1::thin enamel and dentin}}, {{c2::enlarged pulp chambers}}, faint looking.
Teeth with regional odontodysplasia are often non-functional and prone to {{c1::decay or fracture}}; may need extraction.
An odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is a benign but {{c1::aggressive}} cystic odontogenic tumor arising from remnants of the {{c2::dental lamina}}, lined by {{c3::parakeratin}}.
OKCs occur most often in the {{c1::posterior mandible}}, especially the angle and ramus area.
An OKC is a well-defined {{c1::multilocular}} radiolucency that can resorb teeth and displace roots with {{c2::minimal bone expansion}}.
OKCs have a high {{c1::recurrence}} rate due to the presence of {{c2::daughter cysts}}; they need surgical removal.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: OKC = "Oh Keep Coming back!" Often asymptomatic until large.

cloze.text: Multiple OKCs are linked to {{c1::nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome)}}.
A lateral periodontal cyst is a developmental cyst in bone from remnants of the {{c1::dental lamina}}, reduced enamel epithelium, or epithelial rests of Malassez.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: it is NOT pulp-related, unlike periapical cyst/abscess/granuloma — it comes from trapped tooth-related cells in bone.

cloze.text: A lateral periodontal cyst lies on the lateral aspect of a {{c1::vital}} tooth root, commonly between the {{c2::mandibular canine and premolar}}.
A lateral periodontal cyst is a well-circumscribed radiolucency; clinically may be a small, firm swelling of the {{c1::interdental papilla}} or attached gingiva.
cloze.extra: Asymptomatic; surgical enucleation; low recurrence risk.

cloze.text: When a lateral periodontal cyst occurs in soft tissue rather than bone, it is called a {{c1::gingival cyst}}.
An odontoma is a benign tumor composed of fully formed {{c1::enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp}}.
A {{c1::compound}} odontoma appears as a cluster of many small tooth-like structures, typically in the {{c2::anterior maxilla}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: compound = many teeth (2 "o"s = more than two small teeth).

cloze.text: A {{c1::complex}} odontoma is a solid, irregular {{c2::radiopaque}} mass that does not resemble teeth, commonly in the {{c3::posterior mandible}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: complex = one big mass, like a shopping complex.

cloze.text: Odontomas are often asymptomatic but may cause delayed eruption, swelling, or tooth displacement; surgical removal is needed, with {{c1::no risk of recurrence}}.

basic.front: Why is the name "pyogenic granuloma" misleading?
basic.back: It produces no pus ("pyo-") and is not a true granuloma (immune-cell cluster of chronic inflammation) — it is a vascular overgrowth from irritation or trauma.
basic.extra: Fun fact: the name stuck from before microscopes.

basic.front: Why do sialoliths form most often in the submandibular gland?
basic.back: Its duct (Wharton's) is long and curved and travels against gravity, increasing the risk of mineral buildup.
Small fold that anchors and stabilizes oral tissues like the tongue or lips while allowing controlled movement

basic.front: Why is a dry socket so painful?
basic.back: Bone and nerve endings are exposed to air and debris without a protective blood clot, triggering intense inflammation.
basic.extra: Managed with irrigation, dressing, and pain control.

typein.question: An aspirin burn heals spontaneously within how many days once the irritant is removed? (range)
Dry-socket pain typically starts how many days after extraction? (range)
typein.extra: Sharp, radiating pain + bad odor, foul taste.

mcq.question: A patient with HIV presents with a 1.5-cm painful ulcer on the soft palate that has been present for 4 weeks. Which lesion is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Major aphthae are >1 cm, on movable mucosa, take several weeks to heal (often scarring) and are associated with immunodeficiency such as HIV. Minor aphthae are <1 cm and heal in 7–10 days.

mcq.question: Which oral reaction is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity mediated by T-cells?
mcq.explanation: Contact dermatitis is T-cell mediated, appearing hours to days after contact. Urticaria and angioedema are histamine-driven allergic reactions that appear suddenly.

mcq.question: A 52-year-old woman reports dry mouth, gritty dry eyes and bilateral parotid enlargement. Which test would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Panoramic radiograph for a sialolith
B. Minor salivary gland biopsy of the lip
D. Biopsy of the floor of the mouth for a ranula
mcq.answer: B. Minor salivary gland biopsy of the lip
mcq.explanation: Dry mouth + dry eyes + bilateral parotid swelling suggests Sjögren's syndrome, confirmed by lip minor salivary gland biopsy and blood tests (rheumatoid factor/autoantibodies). A sialolith causes unilateral meal-time pain and swelling, usually of the submandibular gland.

mcq.question: A white, corrugated plaque on the lateral border of the tongue that cannot be wiped off is found in a patient with HIV. What is the cause?
options: C. Elongated filiform papillae from keratin buildup
mcq.explanation: This is hairy leukoplakia, caused by EBV (HHV-4) in immunosuppressed patients. Candida (pseudomembranous) wipes off; hairy TONGUE (elongated filiform papillae) is on the dorsum, not the lateral border.

mcq.question: An edentulous patient who sleeps in his maxillary denture has a diffuse red palate exactly outlining the denture base, without nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Denture stomatitis (chronic atrophic candidiasis) is diffuse redness confined to the denture base. Papillary hyperplasia shows red cobblestone projections; epulis fissuratum is folds of fibrous tissue at the denture edge in the vestibule.

mcq.question: A patient has severe throbbing pain, facial swelling, and a tooth that feels high when biting. The radiograph shows only a widened PDL space at the apex. Most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: An acute periapical abscess is severely painful, the tooth feels elevated, and early on shows only a widened PDL space. Granulomas and cysts are asymptomatic chronic lesions with a periapical radiolucency.

mcq.question: A multilocular radiolucency in the posterior mandibular ramus resorbs adjacent roots with little expansion and recurs after removal. The patient also has multiple basal cell carcinomas. Which lesion is it?
mcq.explanation: OKCs are multilocular, aggressive, recur (daughter cysts), favour the posterior mandible, and multiple OKCs indicate Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome. A dentigerous cyst is unilocular and attached to the CEJ of an impacted tooth.

mcq.question: A radiograph of the anterior maxilla shows a cluster of many small tooth-like radiopaque structures blocking eruption of a permanent incisor. Which lesion is this?
mcq.explanation: Compound odontomas are clusters of small tooth-like structures, typically in the anterior maxilla. Complex odontomas are a single irregular radiopaque mass, usually in the posterior mandible.
